rules.rationale: Hydrogen-bond donors (OH, NH) add polar surface area, raising aqueous solubility.
Moderate donor count still adds polar surface, though less than high-donor molecules.
Longer SMILES implies larger molecular size, which typically lowers solubility.
Lack of hydrogen bonding reduces aqueous solubility relative to polar donors.

skills.hypothesis: Polar hydrogen-bond donors raise aqueous solubility, so donor-rich, compact molecules should score highest. Fails if polarity is offset by large hydrophobic surface.

rules.rationale: Ring-rich topology often means rigid, hydrophobic structure, lowering aqueous solubility.
High rotatability usually indicates flexible, non-planar hydrophobic surface, reducing solubility.
Counterintuitively, donor-free apolar molecules can be highly soluble if small and compact.
Very long SMILES encodes huge molecules, which are almost always insoluble.

skills.hypothesis: Ring-rich, flexible hydrophobic topology lowers solubility, so the donor-rich prior may be reversed. Fails if ring-rich molecules are small and polar.

lesson: The ESOL task rewards aqueous solubility, which tracks polar hydrogen-bonding capacity more reliably than ring or rotatable-bond counts. Ring-rich and very-long candidates are rare, so their low-solubility prior carries little information.
revision_summary: Kept the polar-donor solubility mechanism and added a counter-hypothesis that reverses the ring/rotatable prior, both with modest semantic mass decay. Deployed the donor-rich skill because its mechanistic rationale is better grounded in aqueous solubility chemistry.
